##### Summary

### Provides parsing of /proc/pagetypeinfo to provide fragmentation of free memory pages.

The buddyallocator is the system memory allocator: the whole memory space is split
 in **physical pages** (whose size is determined by the CPU Architecture & MMU). These physical pages are grouped into "page groups" of 2^10 (order 10) physical pages. (also numa node & zones).

When the kernel or an application requests some memory, the buddyallocator provides a page that matches closest the request. 
If an application requests 100KB, the buddy allocator will try to find a page of 128KB (order 7: 2^7).
If there is no such order available, it will find a page frm a superior order, and split it in 2 * 128K page. If no super page is available, it will try to reclaim memory from buffer / cache (reclaimable).

In x86, this translates to:  
- each physical page is 4KB,
- minimal size (order 0) of a pagegroup = 4KB
- maximal size (order 10) or a pagegroup = 4MB
- Zone DMA = 24bits: 0 => 16MB
- Zone DMA32 = 32bits: 16MB => 4GB
- Zone Normal = 4GB and up

pagetypeinfo show statistics of free memory available from the buddy allocator.
The sum of all buddyallocator pages must be equal the "Free Memory" from `/proc/meminfo`

##### Component Name

This addition is done in `collectors/proc.plugin`.

##### Additional Information
Closes #6802 

Ideas about configuration items and default values are welcome.

> @vlvkobal @Ferroin what do you think? My opinion is an external collector is better.

External collector has pros and cons.
- Pro: Allows to avoid integrating another optional third-party library (eg, freeipmi, cups, netlink)
- Pro: Allows to grant extended capabilities to restricted binary/code (eg perf, apps)
- Con: increase complexity (new binary, build rules, packaging files...)
- Con: cannot be integrated with netdata.conf (eg, slabinfo has no configuration)

So, should this collector have needed a third party library, or required anything else than a chmod, I would also have been in favor of an external module.
However, the solution here being a chmod to be added either at system startup, or within the service definition, I'd rather keep it within proc.plugin. And also merge the slabinfo module in proc.plugin to be able to have configuation within netdata.conf, especially as its disabled by default.

issue_context.title: Monitor /proc/pagetypeinfo for memory fragmentation
issue_context.body:
##### Feature idea summary
The Linux Kernel splits its memory space in Zones (eg, for x86_64):
- DMA : @ 0 to 16MB, for legacy reasons
- DMA32 : @ 16MB to 4GB, for 32bits hardware
- Normal: @4GB to ..., the standard addressing.

Each of these zones is split in pages of 2^10 (1MB for 4KB pagesize) by the **buddyallocator**.
To limit internal fragmentation, it will try to take the smallest page that satisfy the request.

eg: an application requests 100K. The allocator will search for a page of order 7 (128K). If it can't find one, it will try to search for a higher order (8) and split it in 2 half (buddies). If it still can't, it'll do the same twice with an order 9 page, ... up to the max order.

When a page is released, the allocator will try to merge it with its buddy to form a higher page.

If all pages are low-level pages, it often denotes memory fragmentation. Most of the time, this is due to the kernel cache that uses unmovable pages. You can clean the most consumed (inode & dentries) by issuing a "echo 3 >/proc/sys/vm/drop_caches".

- each graph will have the 10 orders as dimension, named and multiplied by their size (eg, dim0 = 4KB, dim10=1024KB).
- Another stack graph as the distribution of the total memory of the system, between **used** (without detail on the page size, that would need parsing of /proc/*/smaps), and the different pages types.

comments:
The linux buddy allocator fragmentation issue is of very high importance. Long running servers will definitely suffer from it. Some drivers will attempt to `kmalloc()` large regions which may also break the kernel under those circumstances.

I support this feature request in principle, but I have no strong feeling on the specifics of how the graphs must be presented.

I'm currently working on it.
For the graphs I needed by experience, I'm currently doing :

- Global available size per-order: 1 Set (the whole system), 10 dim (the 10 orders). This provides overview of the system global fragmentation
- Detail Per-Numanode & Zone & Type: Type non zero (usually 3: unmovable,movable, reclaimable) * ( Number of NUMA nodes (usually 1 or 2) + 2 (DMA/DMA32 for Node0 only) = 6-8 Sets. 10 Dim each (the 10 orders).  Shows detail on the Type (unmovable, movable, reclaimable) to understand what kind of allocation type is fragmenting the system.

Will try to add some configuration to select the types to be added (forcefully or auto).

> Other types (Reclaimable, HighAtomic, CMA, Isolate) are rarely used and would add dimensions for nothing.

We should at least have the option to have them included, even if they're disabled by default.  CMA is actually used pretty actively on some systems (certain setups on the Raspberry Pi make use of it for example), and fragmentation affecting the Reclaimable pages can be rather important at times.
Yes, that's planned :  With "auto" I will only add types with non-empty pages (to limit useless metrics), and all can be forcefully listed to be added even if empty.
